title: Testing a workplace program to prevent computer vision syndrome (CVS) and dry eye syndrome (DES) in computer users
official: Workplace intervention to prevent computer vision syndrome and dry eye syndrome in video display terminal workers (INTERVIS): protocol for a multicentre cluster-randomised controlled trial
summary:
Background and study aims
The INTERVIS study aims to prevent and reduce two common eye problems associated with prolonged screen use at work: Computer Vision Syndrome (CVS) and Dry Eye Syndrome (DES). These conditions can cause symptoms such as eye strain, dryness, blurred vision, and headaches, and are common among workers who regularly use computers and other screen-based devices. The study will evaluate whether a comprehensive workplace intervention can reduce the frequency of CVS and DES, improve workers’ visual and ocular health and quality of life, and provide good value for the resources required to implement it.

Who can participate?
Employees aged 18–70 years who use video display terminals (VDTs) for at least four hours per workday. Participants must work full time, have worked in the selected work unit for at least one year, be actively employed when the study begins, and provide written informed consent.

What does the study involve?
Work units, rather than individual participants, will be randomly assigned to either the intervention group or the control group. Participants in the control group will continue to receive usual occupational health care.

The intervention will combine several preventive measures, including:
Assessment and improvement of workstation ergonomics, lighting, temperature, and humidity; education on healthy lifestyle and visual habits, including physical activity, diet, appropriate use of dietary supplements, smoking cessation, regular screen breaks, and blinking; optometric and ophthalmological screening to identify CVS, DES, and other visual or ocular problems at an early stage; and individualized recommendations based on each participant’s screening results and risk profile, which may include optical correction, training in the 20-20-20 rule, blinking exercises, or lubricating eye drops when clinically appropriate.

Participants will be followed for three months and will complete questionnaires and undergo visual and ocular assessments at the beginning of the study (T0) and after three months (T1), at the end of the intervention and follow-up period. Quality of life and information on healthcare use and sickness absence will also be collected at both time points to assess the costs and benefits of the intervention.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants may benefit from early identification of visual or ocular problems and from recommendations aimed at improving visual comfort and workplace conditions. However, individual benefit cannot be guaranteed. The study procedures are considered low risk. Some participants may experience minor inconvenience or temporary discomfort during eye examinations or may find the questionnaires and study visits time-consuming.

Where is the study run from?
The study is being conducted at Hospital del Mar in Barcelona and the University of Alicante, Spain.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
January 2027 to July 2027. 

Who is funding the study?
The study is supported through existing institutional resources, facilities, infrastructure and professional time provided by the participating institutions. No specific external or internal financial grant has been awarded to fund the study, and no dedicated funding has been provided for publication costs.
 
Who is the main contact?
Prof. Dr José María Ramada Rodilla, jose.ramada@upf.edu, jramada@hmar.cat

interventions.name:
Current interventions as of 11/11/2026: 
Stratified cluster randomization by study site will be performed to allocate clusters to either the intervention or usual-care control group. Participants in both groups will continue to receive standard occupational health care provided by the Occupational H

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Current key inclusion criteria as of 11/11/2026: 

Selected clusters will consist of independent work units, defined as either a standalone building or a clearly delineated work area within a large building. Eligible participants must be aged 18–70 years, hold a full-time employment contract, have worked in the selected cluster for at least one year, be actively employed at study initiation, and have occupational exposure to video display terminals (VDTs) for at least four hours per workday.

_____

Previous key inclusion criteria as of 28/08/2026: 

Selected clusters will consist of independent work units, defined as either a standalone building or a clearly delineated work area located on a separate floor within the same building. Eligible participants must be aged 18–70 years, hold a full-time employment contract, have worked in the selected cluster for at least one year, be actively employed at study initiation, and have occupational exposure to video display terminals (VDTs) for at least four hours per workday.

_____

Previous key inclusion criteria:

Participants must have been working in the selected cluster (independent building) for at least the last year, hold a full-time contract, and be actively employed at the beginning of the study.
Exclusion criteria:
Current key exclusion criteria as of 11/11/2026: 

1. History of ocular surgery or ocular procedures that may substantially affect the ocular surface, tear film, or visual function
2. Presence of an ocular disease or condition, other than CVS or DES, that may substantially interfere with the assessment of the study outcomes (e.g., amblyopia or clinically significant cataract)
3. Presence of a systemic disease known to substantially affect the ocular surface or tear production, including relevant autoimmune or connective tissue disorders
4. Current use of systemic or topical medications known to substantially affect tear production, tear-film stability, or ocular surface status
5. Any other ophthalmological, systemic, or neurological condition that, in the investigators’ clinical judgment, could substantially interfere with the assessment of CVS or DES or act as a major confounding factor

_____

Previous key exclusion criteria as of 28/08/2026: 

1. History of ocular surgery or ocular procedures that may substantially affect the ocular surface, tear film, or visual function
2. Presence of active ocular disease, other than CVS or DES, that may interfere with the assessment of visual or ocular outcomes
3. Presence of systemic diseases known to substantially affect the ocular surface or tear production, including autoimmune or connective tissue diseases such as Sjögren’s syndrome
4. Current use of systemic or topical medications known to substantially affect tear production, tear-film stability, or ocular surface status
5. Any other ophthalmological, systemic, or neurological condition that, in the investigators’ clinical judgment, could substantially interfere with the assessment of CVS or DES or act as a major confounding factor
6. Inability to complete the study questionnaires or undergo the scheduled optometric and ophthalmological examinations
7. Failure to provide written informed consent

_____

Previous key exclusion criteria:

1. Workers under 18 or over 70 years old
2. Workers not currently employed in the selected cluster (independent building) for at least the past year
3. Workers with part-time contracts
4. Individuals who, although belonging to any of the intervention or control clusters, are not actively employed at the beginning of the study
5. Individuals who do not consent to sign the informed consent document
